result: The authors developed a high-speed volumetric imaging platform for whole-brain fluorescence microscopy. The platform integrates a resonant-scanning two-photon microscope with a vibratome, achieves imaging speeds of 16 million voxels/s (>50 mm³/day), and includes automated control software and computational tools for large-scale image data processing.
evaluation: Claims C5-C47 collectively describe the technical components and performance of the imaging platform. The measured imaging speeds (C36-C37), hardware specifications (C33-C35), and operational workflow (C42-C47) are well-documented with quantitative metrics and supported by figures. The 16-48× speed increase over conventional systems (C39) is appropriately benchmarked.

result: The authors developed a novel tissue clearing method using DMSO, d-sorbitol, and aqueous buffer that preserves fluorescence, enables deep imaging (>200 μm), is compatible with serial sectioning, and remains stable during extended imaging sessions. The method addresses limitations of existing clearing techniques.
evaluation: Claims C48-C82 describe the development and validation of the clearing protocol. The systematic evaluation of existing methods (C55-C62) and the rationale for component selection (C63-C68) are well-justified. Quantitative validation is provided through imaging depth measurements (C75), fluorescence preservation data (C69, Figure 2b,c), and long-term stability tests (C76-C77). The refractive index matching (C70) is supported by Figure 2a.

result: The authors developed a computational pipeline for registering, visualizing, and storing terabyte-scale imaging datasets. The pipeline uses autofluorescent lipofuscin as fiducial markers for submicron-resolution registration across tissue sections and generates multiresolution representations for efficient navigation.
evaluation: Claims C83-C94 describe the computational infrastructure. The data volume calculations (C85-C86) are mathematically sound given the stated voxel size and brain volume. The registration approach using lipofuscin (C90-C91) is validated in Figure 3, showing submicron residual errors. The continuity of neuronal structures across tile boundaries (C94) is demonstrated in Video 1, confirming registration accuracy.

result: The authors achieved sparse, high-intensity neuronal labeling using a dual-virus strategy that labels 10-50 neurons per brain with sufficient brightness for imaging fine axonal collaterals throughout the brain. High excitation power did not degrade resolution, and lossy compression reduced data size by 95% with minimal SNR loss (4.8%).
evaluation: Claims C95-C105 describe the labeling strategy and imaging quality. The viral labeling approach (C95-C96) is well-established and appropriately cited. Quantitative SNR measurements (C103) show consistently high values (15.0 ± 2.9 z-score), supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The compression analysis (C104-C105) demonstrates minimal quality loss with substantial data reduction. High-power imaging without saturation artifacts (C101) is validated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

result: The platform enables reconstruction of long-distance axonal projections with high completeness outside the injection site, despite axonal crossovers at the injection site preventing local reconstruction. Reconstruction throughput (3-12 mm/hour) substantially exceeds classical serial-section methods.
evaluation: Claims C106-C114 address reconstruction feasibility and limitations. The authors transparently acknowledge that high labeling density at the injection site (C110) prevents complete local reconstruction, as shown in Figure 5c. However, long-distance projections are successfully reconstructed (C111), demonstrated in Figure 6a and Video 2. The throughput comparison (C113-C114) is appropriately benchmarked against prior work. The limitation is honestly reported rather than overstated.

result: The authors reconstructed five motor cortex projection neurons (two layer II/III IT, two layer V IT, one layer VI corticothalamic) across a single mouse brain, revealing extensive arborizations (total >300 mm axon length) targeting 28 distinct brain regions. Individual neurons showed surprisingly diverse projection patterns, including a layer V neuron with extensive taenia tecta projections rarely seen in bulk tracing.
evaluation: Claims C8, C32, C115-C127 present the biological findings from the reconstructions. The quantitative measurements (C117-C118, C124-C125, C127) are directly derived from the reconstructions shown in Figures 6-7 and Table 2. The diversity of projections (C116) and the taenia tecta finding (C121-C122) are well-documented. The topographic analysis (C124-C127) provides quantitative evidence for organizational principles. The speculation about continuum vs. discrete targeting (C126) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion.

result: The authors establish the scientific context and motivation for developing whole-brain single-neuron reconstruction methods, citing limitations of bulk tracing methods and prior single-cell reconstruction approaches.
evaluation: Claims C1-C26 provide background and motivation. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations to prior work (C9-C13, C18, C21-C24) and accurately represent the state of the field. The logical progression from bulk methods' limitations (C10-C14) to the need for single-cell approaches (C15-C16) is sound. The technical challenges cited (C22-C24) are well-established in the literature.

result: The authors position their approach relative to alternative imaging technologies (SPIM, knife-edge scanning microscopy, electron microscopy), explaining why STP tomography extended to 3D volumetric imaging addresses limitations of these alternatives for whole-brain axonal reconstruction.
evaluation: Claims C128-C141 provide technical context and comparisons. The limitations of alternative methods (C137-C141) are accurately cited and represent fair assessments supported by the referenced literature. The comparison in Table 3 provides quantitative benchmarking of resolution and speed. The authors appropriately acknowledge that their approach builds on prior STP tomography (C133-C136) while extending it to overcome previous limitations.

result: The authors discuss the fundamental requirement for sparse labeling in light microscopy reconstruction, acknowledge that axonal crossovers cannot be entirely eliminated, and describe the advantages of reconstructing multiple neurons within a single brain for assessing spatial organization.
evaluation: Claims C142-C152 provide methodological discussion and interpretation. The fundamental limitation of optical resolution (C142-C144) is accurately stated and demonstrated in Figure 5c. The discussion of advantages for multi-neuron reconstruction (C148-C151) is logical and well-reasoned. Suggestions for alternative labeling strategies (C146-C147) are appropriately cited and represent reasonable future directions.

result: The authors discuss current limitations (time and storage requirements), future scalability through multiplexing and automation, and position their work within the broader context of connectomics efforts, arguing it fills a gap in available tools for single-neuron whole-brain reconstruction.
evaluation: Claims C153-C165 provide discussion of limitations and future directions. Current limitations (C153-C154) are honestly stated. Future improvements through multiplexing (C155) and automation (C156-C157) are reasonable predictions supported by appropriate citations. The broader context (C158-C163) accurately represents the state of connectomics efforts. The significance claims (C164-C165) are appropriately qualified and represent reasonable assessments of the contribution.
